messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: nested parallelization
parts:
Hi!

I have a bunch of data sets to run my model over and I would love to run everything in parallel. So is there an easy way to parallelize over the different fits and chains in rstan (while still controlling exactly the reproducibility)?

... or am I better off by running Stan chain by chain and then merge as needed?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] nested parallelization
parts:
You just need to specify the same seed and give
each chain a different chain ID. Then you can write
to CSV format and recombine later. It's fully
reproducible. Someone else will have to tell you
how to combine the results --- I think you get a slightly
degenerate fit object as a result (that doesn't have
all the bits).

- Bob

Hi!

Thanks - I was in a rush today and solved the problem by just shortcutting, i.e. Stan gave me great results with only 250 warmup iterations and then the need for parallelization was´t that pressing anymore (per problem was sufficient).

BTW, is 250 still the magic minimum number of iterations I have to use in order to get a mass matrix which is adapted to my problem?

@Bob: I already wrote a couple of scripts which utilize cmdstan and kick off each individual chain on our cluster along with recollecting things afterwards for usage in R - the only drawback is the inflation of files and directories, but I guess I should just improve my scripts.

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] nested parallelization
parts:
> On Oct 27, 2015, at 4:26 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi!
>
> Thanks - I was in a rush today and solved the problem by just shortcutting, i.e. Stan gave me great results with only 250 warmup iterations and then the need for parallelization was´t that pressing anymore (per problem was sufficient).
>
> BTW, is 250 still the magic minimum number of iterations I have to use in order to get a mass matrix which is adapted to my problem?

It's configurable. See the algorithms part of the manual.

And the number of draws you need depends on how easy the posterior
geometry is to move around. If you have a very simple theta ~ normal(0, 1);
model then the initial state's going to be very good as a starting point
and it won't take long at all to adapt.

> @Bob: I already wrote a couple of scripts which utilize cmdstan and kick off each individual chain on our cluster along with recollecting things afterwards for usage in R - the only drawback is the inflation of files and directories, but I guess I should just improve my scripts.

I think that goes with the clustering territory --- you could
always run everything in something like Hadoop which would check
jobs being up and help combine the results if you want to
encapsulate all the back and forth.

- Bob
